title: Stale Product Cache
description:
## Stale Product Cache

You're on-call for a **product catalog service** built in Python. The service uses **Redis** as a read-through cache in front of **Postgres**.

Users are reporting that after updating a product's details (e.g., price or name), the **old values continue to appear** when they read the product back. The stale data eventually disappears but only after a very long time.

A load generator is continuously simulating a mix of read and write traffic against the catalog service, making the problem clearly visible.

### Your Task
- Investigate the product catalog service's read and write paths.
- Identify why stale data persists in reads after a product is updated.
- Apply a fix so that reads always reflect the most recent write.

### Hints
- Look at how the service handles caching on the **write path**.
- Consider what should happen to the cached entry when a product is updated.

problemStatement.overview: The product catalog service uses a cache-aside pattern with Redis in front of Postgres. After a product is updated, stale cached values continue to be served to readers because the write path never invalidates the Redis key.
problemStatement.brokenState: The product-catalog-service's write/update handler updates the product row in Postgres but does NOT invalidate or update the corresponding Redis cache entry. The cache has a very long TTL (3600 seconds), so subsequent reads continue to serve the stale cached value until it naturally expires.
problemStatement.yourTask: Investigate the product catalog service's read and write paths. Identify why stale data persists in reads after a product is updated. Apply a fix so that reads always reflect the most recent write.
hints: Look at how the service handles caching on the write path.
Consider what should happen to the cached entry when a product is updated.
The fix is a one-liner: delete (or update) the Redis key inside the PUT handler.

cmd: wget -qO- http://localhost:5000/products/2 > /tmp/before_update.json && cat /tmp/before_update.json && wget -qO- --post-data='{"name":"VALIDATION_SENTINEL_NAME","price":"1234.56"}' --header='Content-Type: application/json' http://localhost:5000/products/2 && sleep 0.1 && wget -qO- http://localhost:5000/products/2 > /tmp/after_update.json && cat /tmp/after_update.json && grep -c 'VALIDATION_SENTINEL_NAME' /tmp/after_update.json || echo 'STALE_CONFIRMED: read returned old cached value after write'

wget -qO- --post-data='{"name":"StaleTestProduct","price":"777.77"}' --header='Content-Type: application/json' http://localhost:5000/products/3 && sleep 0.1 && RESULT=$(wget -qO- http://localhost:5000/products/3) && echo "$RESULT" && echo "$RESULT" | grep -q 'StaleTestProduct' && echo 'NOT_STALE' || echo 'STALE_BUG_CONFIRMED'

arch: The load-generator sends a mix of read (GET) and write (PUT) requests to the product-catalog-service. The product-catalog-service implements a cache-aside pattern: on reads it checks Redis first, falling back to Postgres and populating the cache on a miss. On writes it updates Postgres. All three backing services (product-catalog-service, Redis, Postgres) are networked together.

display.guidance: No metrics panel for this challenge. The staleness is observable directly through the load generator's output or by manually querying the read endpoint after a write.
